notes.h: Classes of retail outlet (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Retail outlets are grouped by ownership, range of goods and pricing policy.
points: Independent retailer: a single, locally owned shop, such as a butcher, jeweller or boutique, offering personal service and a specialised range.
Chain store (multiple retailer): several outlets under one owner, selling a standard range and buying in bulk, such as Penneys.
Supermarket: a self-service store selling a wide range of food and household goods, such as Tesco or SuperValu.
Department store: a large store divided into departments selling clothing, household goods and cosmetics, such as Brown Thomas or Arnotts.
Discount store: a store selling a limited range at low prices, kept low by minimal service and fast turnover of stock, such as Dealz.
Mail-order or online retailer: sells from a catalogue or website and delivers to the consumer's home, such as ASOS.
Market stall or farmers' market: small-scale direct selling, often by producers, typically of fresh produce.
Independent retailers compete on personal service and specialist knowledge, while chains and supermarkets compete on range and price.

notes.b: Retailers design the shopping environment around how people perceive value, risk and time.
points: Impulse buying: an unplanned purchase triggered by a display, a special offer or a product seen at the checkout.
Perceived value: shoppers judge a price against a reference price, so a 'was' price makes a reduction seem a bargain even when the saving is small.
Relaxed shoppers browse for longer and so see and buy more products.
Perceived risk: consumers hesitate over unfamiliar products, so a known brand reduces the risk they feel in buying.
Limited time and attention: shoppers rely on quick cues such as colour, packaging and brand names rather than reading every label.
Scarcity and urgency: labels such as 'limited offer' encourage a purchase now rather than later.
Social proof: displays showing many units, or a 'best seller' label, suggest that other people approve of the product.

notes.h: Changes in shopping patterns (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Shopping patterns have changed in response to time pressure, technology and changing values.
points: Frequency: many households have moved from a single weekly bulk shop to several smaller top-up trips.
One-stop shopping: large out-of-town centres sell food, clothing and services under one roof.
Extended hours: late-night, Sunday and 24-hour opening give shoppers more flexibility.
Online, television and social media shopping: consumers order through websites, apps, TV shopping channels and social media, often with home delivery.
Payment: cash has been largely replaced by debit cards, contactless payment and mobile payment apps.
Self-checkout and scan-as-you-go systems let shoppers bypass the checkout queue.
Resale and second-hand trade: charity shops, vintage stores and online resale platforms have grown as shoppers seek value and reduce waste.
Drivers of change: time pressure, budget, health and special diets, family structure, and environmental and ethical values.

notes.h: Consumer research: desk and field research (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Consumer research gathers information about what consumers want, how they buy, and how large a market is.
points: Purpose: research identifies consumer wants and expectations, tests the market before a product is launched, and highlights trends, market size and potential markets.
Desk research uses existing (secondary) information, such as reports from state agencies, Central Statistics Office data and internet sources.
Desk research is quick to carry out, relatively inexpensive, and can cover a large amount of information.
Desk research is general and quantitative, so it shows what people do rather than why, and it may not answer a specific question about a product.
Field research collects new (primary) information directly from consumers through observation, interviews, surveys, vox pops, consumer panels and focus groups.
Field research is qualitative and detailed, showing attitudes, preferences and reasons for buying, but it takes longer and costs more.
A vox pop is a short, informal interview with members of the public in a public place, used to gather opinions quickly.
A consumer panel is a fixed group of consumers who report on products over time; a focus group is a guided discussion with a small group about a product.
Loyalty card data and application forms record buying habits and personal details, which retailers use as a research source.

notes.h: Uses of consumer research (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Research benefits both the retailer and the consumer.
points: Retailer: research identifies the type of person likely to buy a product.
Retailer: research shows whether a product meets consumer requirements, and shows the size and location of the market.
Manufacturer: research shows what consumers will buy before production is committed.
Consumer: research identifies what consumers need, so that products can be improved in quality.
Consumer: competition between retailers informed by research can help keep prices down.

factCards.term: Three advantages of gathering information from published sources
factCards.definition: Large amounts of information can be collected quickly, it is relatively inexpensive, and it needs no direct contact with consumers.

factCards.term: Three limitations of relying on published sources for market information
factCards.definition: The information is general rather than detailed, it is quantitative so it shows what people do rather than why, and it may not answer a specific question about a product.

factCards.term: Four methods of collecting new information from consumers
factCards.definition: Observation, interviews, surveys and vox pops.

factCards.term: Three benefits of research to a retailer
factCards.definition: It identifies the type of person likely to buy, shows whether a product meets requirements, and shows the size and location of the market.
A self-service layout and a wide range of food and household goods.

questions.prompt: Describe the main features of two classes of retail outlet, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Two classes, each with a feature and an example. Independent retailer: a single, locally owned shop with personal service and a specialist range, such as a butcher or jeweller. Department store: a large store divided into departments selling clothing, household goods and cosmetics, such as Brown Thomas. Other acceptable answers include supermarket, chain store, discount store and mail-order or online retailer, each with a correct feature and a correct example.

questions.prompt: Analyse how changes in shopping patterns affect consumers and retailers, and explain how consumer research helps a retailer respond to these changes.
questions.model: Changes in shopping patterns: more frequent top-up trips, one-stop shopping in large centres, extended and 24-hour opening, online, television and social media shopping with home delivery, cashless payment and self-checkout, and growth of resale. Effects on consumers: more choice and convenience, but greater risk of overspending and of payment fraud online. Effects on retailers: need to offer online ordering and delivery, to extend hours, and to compete on range and convenience, while smaller independent shops may lose trade. Consumer research: desk research uses existing data, such as state agency reports and Central Statistics Office figures, to show market trends and size quickly and cheaply; field research uses surveys, interviews, focus groups and consumer panels to find out why consumers are changing their habits. Together they show a retailer which products to stock, what type of customer to target, and where to locate or sell. A complete answer links each change to a consumer or retailer effect and shows how a named research method would reveal it.
